title: Euclid’s view of the Horsehead Nebula
caption: The Horsehead Nebula, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: Horsehead Nebula, Barnard 33 · constellation Orion · about 1,375 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: One of Euclid’s first five full-color images (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The dark, horse-head-shaped cloud of the Horsehead Nebula stands out in this wide, crisp view from ESA’s Euclid space telescope. Also called Barnard 33, it lies about 1,375 light-years away in Orion, just south of Alnitak, the easternmost of the three stars in Orion’s Belt.

The Horsehead is part of the vast Orion molecular cloud, and its neighborhood is the closest giant star-forming region to Earth. Plenty of telescopes have photographed it, but none has caught it this sharply across such a wide field in a single observation.

Euclid needed only about an hour. That speed is the point: the mission was built to sweep up large stretches of sky in fine detail, and this was one of its first demonstrations. In its palette, hot stars look white-blue, glowing hydrogen appears blue, and regions rich in dust and molecular gas turn red, while very distant galaxies in the background look deep red.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 1,375 light-years, the frame spans roughly 16 × 16 light-years. Its light set out about 1,375 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: Euclid’s two instruments together cover four wavelength ranges; three were chosen for this color image. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
alt: The dark, horse-head-shaped Horsehead Nebula against reddish clouds of dust and gas, in a wide field full of stars.
